overview: An early Eocene radiation whose initially similar branches diverged into horses, tapirs, rhinoceroses and many extinct groups; the profile treats that history as a branching record, not a ladder.

ecology.habitat: Lineage-specific terrestrial habitats; no single order-wide habitat
ecology.locomotion: Terrestrial, with strongly divergent limb specializations
ecology.bodySize: Small early forms to giant rhinocerotoids
ecology.guild: Browsers, mixed feeders and grazers in separate lineages

traits: Early branches distinguished by subtle dental and cranial characters
Strong lineage-specific divergence of skull, dentition and limbs
evidenceSummary: Tissier and Smith constrain the earliest sampled radiation and dispersal; Prothero synthesizes the broader fossil branching pattern. Neither source supplies an exact origin date or one ecology for the whole order.

overview: An Eocene perissodactyl family revised at species level, with shared cranial and molar traits but substantial variation in size and cranial appendages.

ecology.diet: Herbivorous; folivory supported for sampled teeth
ecology.habitat: Terrestrial Eocene localities; family-wide habitat not generalized
ecology.bodySize: Small early forms to rhinoceros-sized taxa
ecology.guild: Leaf-browser signal in sampled dental evidence

traits: Anteroposteriorly shortened face
Elongate postorbital cranium
Bunoselenodont upper molars with a W-shaped ectoloph
Frontonasal appendages in some, not all, species
evidenceSummary: Mihlbachler’s monograph supplies the taxonomy, morphology and distribution. Dispersal direction and deeper placement remain inferred, and neither giant size nor horns define every species.

geography: Western Europe (French and British study records)
overview: A western European palaeothere represented here by dental-wear evidence from Palaeotherium medium and regional terminal records near the Grande Coupure.

ecology.diet: Leaf browsing with a smaller fruit or abrasive-seed component in sampled P. medium
ecology.habitat: Late Eocene terrestrial locality; habitat not inferred from wear alone
ecology.locomotion: Terrestrial; gait not evaluated in the cited wear study
ecology.bodySize: P. medium sample; genus-wide size not generalized
ecology.guild: Leaf browser in the sampled population

traits: High molar occlusal relief
Mixed sharp and rounded worn cusps
Wear facets consistent with shearing and grinding plant foods
evidenceSummary: Joomun and colleagues directly analyze one species and locality; Hooker and colleagues provide a separate British regional range chart. The profile does not generalize limb form, diet or extinction instant to every species.

geography: Badlands National Park, South Dakota (sampled M. planifrons)
overview: An amynodontid represented by a comparative anatomical test of semi-aquatic locomotion in Metamynodon planifrons, not by a family-wide “swamp rhino” label.

ecology.diet: Herbivorous; diet not tested in the locomotor study
ecology.locomotion: Semi-aquatic inference from comparative anatomy and deposits
ecology.bodySize: Large M. planifrons sample; genus-wide mass not generalized
ecology.guild: No feeding guild assigned beyond the bounded locomotor inference

traits: High-positioned orbits
Reduced thoracic neural spines
Limb-lever proportions differing from more terrestrial amynodontids
evidenceSummary: Wall and Heinbaugh compare orbital, axial and limb characters with other amynodontids. Anatomy and sedimentary association support but do not directly observe behavior.

overview: An Oligocene Asian paraceratheriid genus whose 26.5 Ma Linxia skull and vertebrae refine species relationships and a Tibetan-region dispersal hypothesis.

ecology.diet: Large terrestrial herbivore; feeding height inferred from neck and body form
ecology.habitat: Oligocene Asian woodland–grassland mosaics; locality dependent
ecology.locomotion: Long-limbed terrestrial giant, not elephant-like graviportal
ecology.guild: Large browser inference; direct diet was not measured

traits: Giant skull and body size
Long, flexible neck supported by cervical anatomy
Long rather than stubby graviportal limbs
Species-level cranial and dental diagnoses
evidenceSummary: Deng and colleagues provide the dated specimen, diagnosis, 155-character analysis and occurrence map. Dispersal route, palaeoelevation and feeding height remain inferences.

overview: A genus-level profile bounded to dental-wear samples labelled Chalicotherium goldfussi and the historical combination Chalicotherium (Anisodon) grande.

ecology.diet: Browse-dominated feeding with abrasive bark or twig components
ecology.habitat: Sampled Miocene southern German localities; habitat not inferred from diet alone
ecology.locomotion: Posture reconstructed from limb anatomy, not observed behavior
ecology.bodySize: Large chalicotheriine; no genus-wide mass estimate

traits: Large ungual phalanges interpreted as claws
Short hind limbs in sampled chalicotheriines
Posture and claw function remain functional reconstructions
evidenceSummary: The primary study combines mesowear and microwear and states its historical taxonomy. Dietary evidence is direct; posture and claw use remain interpretations.

geography: Central and western Europe (MN3–MN9 record discussed)
overview: A Miocene equid represented here by A. aurelianense at Sandelzhausen and the regional European MN3–MN9 record, not a single global genus ecology.

ecology.habitat: Warm-temperate woodland context; one-locality dietary sample
ecology.locomotion: Tridactyl terrestrial; cursorial performance not tested
ecology.bodySize: Larger than preceding equids; no single genus-wide mass
ecology.guild: “Dirty browser” or mixed feeder in the sampled population

traits: Low-crowned lophodont cheek teeth
Tridactyl manus with reduced fifth metacarpal
Dental wear more abrasive than a pure-browser model predicts
evidenceSummary: Kaiser analyzes 35 cheek teeth and provides the diagnosis and European biochronology. The profile keeps diet at the sampled species and locality level.

regionalRanges.label: North American tribe-level range
regionalRanges.basis: The North American hipparionin radiation begins near 17 Ma and the classic four-genus synthesis extends to about 2 Ma; exact endpoints remain pending a revised genus-level synthesis.

regionalRanges.label: Old World first dispersal
regionalRanges.basis: The oldest well-supported Old World dispersal window is represented by early Hippotherium records in the Vienna Basin.

regionalRanges.label: Latest Old World regional records
regionalRanges.basis: Terminal records vary by lineage and region; the review places the latest Chinese and African hipparionins around or below 1 Ma rather than at the Holocene boundary.

overview: A persistently tridactyl equine tribe whose Old World radiation comprised multiple genus-rank clades rather than a single broadly defined Hipparion.

ecology.habitat: Forest, woodland and open settings depending on lineage and time
ecology.locomotion: Terrestrial equine locomotion with persistent side toes

traits: Persistent tridactyly
Hypsodont teeth in many lineages
Substantial body-size and dietary variation
evidenceSummary: McHorse and colleagues synthesize foot evolution and North American context; Bernor and colleagues resolve Old World genus-rank ranges, geography, body mass and diet.

overview: A North American rhinoceros with locality-dependent isotope evidence: principally terrestrial Florida populations contrast with limited-mobility, wet-habitat T. major at Ashfall.

ecology.diet: Grazing or mixed feeding depending on locality
ecology.habitat: Open Florida settings and the Ashfall watering-hole landscape
ecology.locomotion: Terrestrial to locally semi-aquatic; genus-wide behavior unresolved

traits: Shortened limb and foot bones
Barrel-bodied T. major at Ashfall
Hypsodont molars
Sexually dimorphic lower second incisors
evidenceSummary: Florida and Ashfall primary studies differ in ecological signal. Body shape alone is not used to choose one genus-wide behavior, and the strongest Ashfall result remains species- and locality-bounded.

overview: A rhinoceros genus with species- and region-specific paleoecology, from Tibetan and East Asian forms to the northern Eurasian woolly rhinoceros C. antiquitatis.

ecology.diet: Typical grazing in C. antiquitatis; mixed feeding in some C. nihowanensis samples
ecology.habitat: Cold dry steppe for C. antiquitatis; other species and regions vary
ecology.bodySize: Large; about 2900 kg reviewed for C. antiquitatis
ecology.guild: Cold-steppe grazer in C. antiquitatis, not a genus-wide constant

traits: Long hair and dense underwool in C. antiquitatis
Low head posture and long nasal horn in C. antiquitatis
High-crowned teeth associated with abrasive grazing
evidenceSummary: Ma and colleagues synthesize isotopic and morphological evidence across species. The 14.4 ka genome constrains one late C. antiquitatis individual and is not used to support morphology, ecology or an exact global extinction boundary.
